general.temas: The disruption to flights in the United States and its consequences feature in four newspapers. Judicial and political matters linked to the Supreme Federal Court (STF) also recur, as do issues concerning health and Brazil’s public health system. Only O Globo highlights the dispute over the Ministry of Culture.
general.motivo_crispacion: Tension is concentrated in Gilmar Mendes’s accusations against Sergio Moro and the dispute over the management of the Ministry of Culture, which has pitted artists against supporters of the minister on social media. Police reports on STF justices and Marco Rubio’s attacks on the International Criminal Court are also generating controversy. Electoral harassment in the workplace reflects another source of conflict. News about health, culture, food and the technical failure in aviation partly offsets that atmosphere.

Folha de S.Paulo.resumen:
- Health: poorly controlled diabetes can cause erectile dysfunction; the front page also highlights the shortage of orthopedic specialists who work exclusively in the public system.
- Energy transition: the high cost of capital makes it difficult to reduce Brazil’s dependence on fossil fuels.
- Politics and justice: Raquel Lyra is moving closer to Lula’s allies; a study examines compensation for electoral harassment at work.
- Society and culture: topics include Brazilian migration to China, screen time, the distribution of wealth across generations and a novel about Korean immigration.
- Also included are the rain forecast for São Paulo, a profile of Lori Huang and the auction of decorative objects from Banco Master and Will Bank.
Folha de S.Paulo.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly informative, although expressions such as “only 4%” and “young people gain ground on income” emphasize scarcity and the generational contrast, without resorting to disparagement or a people-versus-elites divide.
Folha de S.Paulo.sesgo: The selection combines health, economic, political and everyday-life topics, with attention to inequalities and the limitations of public services. No clear partisan leaning is apparent in the headlines provided.

O Globo.resumen:
- The dispute over the management of the Ministry of Culture has prompted mutual accusations on social media.
- Douglas Ruas announces appointments for public security and Rio’s Civil Police, one of which surprises reserve officers.
- More than 3,000 flights remain canceled in the United States after an air traffic disruption.
- The front page includes stories about Deborah Blando, a documentary about Cacá Diegues, a novel and food festivals.
- It also covers exercise, condom use, hugs and a book from 1579 compared with TikTok content.
O Globo.motivo_populismo: The headline about Culture emphasizes the confrontation with “racism vs. cultural Stalinism” and “war on social media,” while others use eye-catching phrases, although informative headlines predominate.
O Globo.sesgo: The front page combines current affairs with culture, entertainment and practical advice. The conflict over Culture is presented in polarized terms, but the coverage as a whole shows no clear political bias.

O Estado de S. Paulo.resumen:
- Trump will discuss Iran with Xi and Putin at the APEC summit.
- Ecuador attributes the plot to attack Daniel Noboa to a criminal protected by Colombian rebels.
- The suspension of takeoffs in the United States ended after more than four hours; the Trump administration blamed an “old system.”
- The front page covers the Banco do Brasil problem, the role of the Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES) during fiscal adjustment and the Unified Health System (SUS) in the face of AI in healthcare.
- It includes articles about a candidacy, the review of a criminal conviction, God and the poor, as well as the readers’ forum.
O Estado de S. Paulo.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly informative, although “Banco do Brasil’s hole is deeper” uses an evocative metaphor; there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
O Estado de S. Paulo.sesgo: The selection prioritizes international politics, the economy and Brazilian institutions, alongside opinion pages. The headlines do not allow a clear political leaning to be identified.

Gazeta do Povo.resumen:
- A communications failure brought flights in the United States to a halt; departures resumed and the FBI is investigating the causes.
- The STF has four votes on ending the six-days-on, one-day-off work schedule; decisions and actions related to Operation Car Wash, Bolsonaro and the court’s justices are also highlighted.
- The Civil Police are investigating a network that provided Brazilian identities to foreigners, including Russians.
- Pope Leo XIV defends university autonomy from the market and celebrates Mass in the Peruvian diocese he once led.
- Democrats seek a pact on the presidential vote in the United States; a family from Paraná stands out for its specialty coffee production.
Gazeta do Povo.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly informative, although expressions such as “neutralize,” “cannot bow down” and “prevent reports from disappearing” add drama; there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
Gazeta do Povo.sesgo: The selection prioritizes Brazilian judicial and institutional matters, alongside the air travel disruption in the United States. It also gives space to the pope’s activities and ideas, without an unambiguous political leaning being apparent in the coverage as a whole.

CartaCapital.resumen:
- The United States resumed flights after a four-hour disruption; authorities ruled out a threat and Brazil’s National Civil Aviation Agency (Anac) advised passengers.
- Rubio again criticized the International Criminal Court, while Gilmar Mendes harshly rejected Moro’s account of the triplex apartment.
- The government did not renew a subsidy for imported diesel, but maintained support for diesel used in road transport.
- One column questions gas policy and another highlights Benedita da Silva’s career; Brazil’s Labor Prosecution Service (MPT) is seeking compensation over hot working conditions at Atacadão.
- In sports, the coverage reports on a penalty imposed on Owono, a Botafogo training session and a court ruling on Vasco’s elections.
CartaCapital.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly informative, although disparaging expressions attributed to Gilmar Mendes appear, such as “delusion” and “vile intentions,” as well as value judgments in the columns.
CartaCapital.sesgo: The selection combines news reporting with opinions advocating greater state planning in the gas sector and celebrating Benedita da Silva’s career and the presence of Black women in power. The coverage also pays attention to working conditions.

opiniones.comunista:
I see the same struggle in today’s news: who pays the cost of organizing the economy for private benefit. Only 3.8% of orthopedic specialists work exclusively in the SUS, even though it is the only healthcare option for about 75% of Brazilians. It is not enough to announce that waiting lists will be reduced: I advocate sustained investment, better working conditions and a public network capable of guaranteeing care regardless of ability to pay.

The energy transition is also hampered by the high cost of capital. In my view, leaving it in investors’ hands means making a collective need subject to their expectations of profitability. I prefer public financing, democratic planning and collective ownership of strategic sectors: the working class must decide on the energy and healthcare it needs.
opiniones.anarquista:
It troubles me that electoral harassment at work is treated as a matter of compensation payments, when it reveals a deeper problem: someone who depends on a wage is hardly free in the face of pressure from their employer. And reports of workers subjected to temperatures of up to 32 °C are a reminder that obedience can also take a toll on health. I do not want to swap a boss for an official making decisions from above: I want workplaces managed by the people who work in them, able to protect themselves through organization and mutual aid.

We are also told that the cost of capital makes it difficult to move away from fossil fuels. If the transition depends on the financial sector deeming it profitable, our collective freedom is subordinated to its priorities. I prefer communities that decide on and manage the energy they need together, without waiting for permission from parties or major property owners.
opiniones.liberal:
The difficulty of accessing cheap capital makes Brazil’s energy transition more expensive. I would not respond with more subsidies and privileges, but with stable rules, fewer barriers and a lower tax burden that allows people to save and invest. Competition can find solutions that no government knows in advance.

That is why I welcome the decision not to renew the subsidy for imported diesel, even though another subsidy for road diesel remains in place. Subsidies shift costs onto taxpayers and distort decisions; eliminating them does, however, require giving those who must adapt a predictable environment. I prefer a limited state that guarantees fair rules and the freedom to do business, alongside citizens and companies responsible for their choices. The transition will be stronger if it is supported by productive investment, not political favors.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
The dismantling of a network that sold Brazilian identities to foreigners reminds me that sovereignty begins with knowing who enters our country and who obtains our documents. I support strict immigration controls and relentless scrutiny of civil registries. Hospitality must not become naivety, nor the right to immigrate an open door to fraud.

I also distrust the elites who present the energy transition as an unquestionable imperative while the high cost of capital makes investment more expensive. Brazil needs affordable energy and the ability to make its own decisions, not commitments that sacrifice its industry and energy security. And I welcome the pope’s reminder that universities should not submit to the immediate demands of the market: a nation needs to pass on its culture and values, not just train workers.
opiniones.centro:
I see two challenges in today’s news that call for fewer slogans and more agreements. The high cost of capital makes Brazil’s energy transition more difficult. I do not believe it is enough to wait for the market or promise unlimited subsidies: what is needed is stable rules, well-designed financing and a transparent assessment of its costs and results. The state should guide investment without unnecessarily replacing private initiative.

I am also concerned that only 3.8% of orthopedic specialists work exclusively in the SUS, while the public system is the only option for a large part of the population. Reducing waiting lists requires negotiating better incentives and cooperation between healthcare networks, without losing sight of fiscal responsibility. I prefer gradual reforms that can be sustained and corrected to spectacular promises that institutions are in no position to fulfill.
